title: Christian Lundgaard was the 'obvious' choice to replace Scott Dixon at Chip Ganassi Racing
excerpt:
Arguably the worst kept secret in racing over the past couple months was that Christian Lundgaard was taking over the vacant seat at Chip Ganassi Racing left by Scott Dixon.

Dixon, a six-time IndyCar champion, essentially completed a swap between CGR and Arrow-McLaren, moving to McLaren after 24 seasons at Ganassi.

Lundgaard was officially announced as the driver of the No. 9 Honda for 2027 on Tuesday.

Lundgaard will join 21-year-old Kyffin Simpson and five-time IndyCar champion Alex Palou at Ganassi. Lundgaard is coming off a career year in 2026 that saw him win two races and finish third in the IndyCar standings.

"I think the first thought that I had when this came on the table and became an opportunity was, I am learning from the best driver who learned from the best driver in Scott Dixon," Lundgaard said on a media call Tuesday, "And I think just getting to learn as much as I can from there. And obviously joining CGR and Chip and the 18 championships, it's really just a dream come true in many ways.

"It's one of those opportunities you never expected to rise, and I'm just super excited to join Chip Ganassi and PNC Bank."

With Palou and Lundgaard racing together as teammates, CGR will have arguably the best duo in all of IndyCar racing next season.

Why Chip Ganassi wanted Christian Lundgaard

"Obviously we looked at everybody," Ganassi said. "You look at everybody that's available. I mean, yeah, we obviously looked at everybody that was out there and available... But Christian's name kept landing back as the obvious one. Like wait a minute, we're not overlooking this guy, are we?

"Every name that came along, we said, okay, well, how does that compare with Lundgaard, whether it's somebody who hasn't been in the series, and did they have to learn the tracks, and are they current with this type of drive style that you need, or are they committed to maybe coming to the U.S."

Of course, Lundgaard won't be filling the shoes of any driver. Dixon won 58 races, six titles and 32 poles while driving for CGR. While he struggled to find pace in 2026, his legacy with the team is giant and unshakeable.

Those numbers will inevitably put Lundgaard under a microscope throughout his tenure with the organization.

"We just look for people with talent," Ganassi said. "I think everything else can sort of be taught. You saw at the end of last season at Milwaukee, he was obviously doing very well on ovals. I think it all has to do with his prerequisites — before being at Ganassi, his prerequisites, he's taken something away from all of those to develop into the driver that he is today. So he has five years of experience in the series. He's been to the Indianapolis 500 now a handful of times.

"These are all things that are no small thing when you're coming into a new environment that make you attractive to a new team. And he seems to be able to keep the car on the — he keeps the rubber side down and the shiny side up, as they say. He keeps the car on the track, so that develops into points. And as you know, we like those guys that can amass points."

Time will tell if Lundgaard can build a comparable legacy to Dixon, but it'd be surprising if he's not immediately in contention for race wins and championships at CGR beginning next season.

Quotes provided by IndyCar Media.

title: Gordon Johncock, 2-time Indy 500 winner, dies at 90
excerpt:
Gordon Johncock, a two-time Indianapolis 500 winner, died on Monday at his home in South Branch, Mich. He was 90.

He won the Indy 500 in 1973 and 1982 and finished with 25 victories, had 20 career poles and 76 podium finishes in open-wheel racing from 1964-83. He also made 21 starts in the NASCAR Cup Series in the 1960s and 1970s but was never a full-time driver.

At age 55, Johncock made his 24th and final start in the Indy 500 in 1992. Only A.J. Foyt, who was 57 for that same race in 1992, was older when he started the prestigious race.

Johncock was inducted into the Indianapolis Motor Speedway Hall of Fame in 1997, the International Motorsports Hall of Fame in 1999 and the Motorsports Hall of Fame of America in 2002.

title: 1 day ago •Driver News Ganassi Signs Christian Lundgaard To Drive No. 9 in Multiyear Deal The newest addition to Chip Ganassi Racing's driver lineup (photo) finished a career-best third in the NTT INDYCAR SERIES standings in 2026, with two race victories.
excerpt:
Driver News

1 day ago

Chip Ganassi Racing (CGR) has signed Danish driver Christian Lundgaard to a multiyear contract to drive the No. 9 PNC Bank Honda in the NTT INDYCAR SERIES starting in the 2027 season.

Three-time INDYCAR SERIES race winner Lundgaard (photo, above) has 16 podium finishes and 21 top-five finishes in 87 career starts. In 2026, he won races at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway road course and at Road America, and he secured a career-best third-place finish in the INDYCAR SERIES championship standings.

Lundgaard will join teammates Alex Palou and Kyffin Simpson as part of the CGR’s 2027 driver lineup. He is replacing Scott Dixon, who left CGR after 24 full-time seasons and six series championships to join Arrow McLaren in 2027.

“It is an honor and a privilege to join Chip Ganassi Racing beginning next season,” Lundgaard said. “The fact that it is in the iconic No. 9 PNC Bank Honda makes it even more special. CGR has set the standard in INDYCAR for decades, and the opportunity to be part of that legacy is something I've worked toward my entire career.

“I'm incredibly excited about what's ahead. I can't wait to get to work with everyone at Chip Ganassi Racing and compete for wins, championships and the Indianapolis 500.”

Lundgaard, 25, has quickly become a well-rounded INDYCAR SERIES talent, scoring victories on both road and street circuits and scoring his first oval podium result in 2026. He was a winning driver in Formula 2 – one step below Formula One – and served briefly a simulator driver for the Alpine F1 Team before coming to the INDYCAR SERIES in 2021 with Rahal Letterman Lanigan Racing. He earned his first victory in 2023 at Toronto with RLL before joining Arrow McLaren in 2025.

“We are excited to welcome Christian to Chip Ganassi Racing,” team owner Chip Ganassi said. “We know he's capable of accomplishing even more in the NTT INDYCAR SERIES, and we're looking forward to helping him reach that next level with the No. 9 team.

“He's already proven he can win races, and it isn't often a driver of his caliber becomes available. Throughout our history, one of the things we've done best is identify young talent, help them maximize their potential and develop them into championship contenders. We believe Christian has all the talent to be the next driver to do that.”

PNC Bank will continue its longstanding partnership with CGR on the No. 9 PNC Bank Honda next season. PNC Bank has been a partner of the team since 2013 and a primary partner on the No. 9 since 2018. With approximately 2,300 branches and 58,000 employees, PNC is one of the largest financial institutions in the U.S.

“We are excited to begin a new era with Chip Ganassi Racing and what’s ahead with Christian taking the wheel of the No. 9 PNC Bank Honda,” said Lou Cestello, PNC Bank head of regional presidents. “He’s already achieved some remarkable milestones early in his career, and we’re looking forward to watching him build on that success in 2027 and beyond.”

The 2027 NTT INDYCAR SERIES season starts Sunday, March 7 on the streets of St. Petersburg, Florida.

title: 1 day ago •Team News Edward Jones, McLaren Announce Multiyear Partnership
excerpt:
Team News

1 day ago

Scott Dixon To Drive No. 6 Edward Jones Arrow McLaren Chevrolet at Indy 500

Edward Jones and McLaren Racing announced Sept. 28 a new, multiyear partnership naming Edward Jones the Official Private Wealth Management Partner of McLaren Racing, spanning the McLaren Mastercard Formula 1 Team and the Arrow McLaren IndyCar Team.

The agreement launches a long-term relationship between McLaren Racing and one of the most trusted financial services firms in North America.

“Edward Jones has a long history of supporting its clients and communities, and we’re excited to welcome them as McLaren Racing partners,” McLaren Racing CEO Zak Brown said. “We have a shared commitment toward preparation and continuous improvement through a people-first culture, making this partnership a natural fit.”

Edward Jones’ activation begins within the 2026 Formula One season and expands to the Arrow McLaren IndyCar Team starting in 2027, giving the firm a year-round motorsports presence across two of the world's premier motorsports platforms.

With Arrow McLaren, Edward Jones will serve as primary partner on the No. 6 Edward Jones Arrow McLaren Chevrolet entry at the 111th Running of the Indianapolis 500 presented by Gainbridge and additional select races. Team newcomer Scott Dixon (photo, top), a six-time series champion, will drive the No. 6 car for the entire season.

Through the partnership, Edward Jones, headquartered in St. Louis, will engage clients, communities and fans through experiences, storytelling and programming that highlight the values at the heart of both organizations: preparation, teamwork, resilience and performance. The relationship also includes co-branded content across McLaren Racing’s digital and social channels.

“Whether on a racetrack or in a financial plan, success is rarely the result of a single moment; instead, it’s built through preparation, discipline and thousands of decisions made over time, said Hema Widhani, Edward Jones principal and chief brand, experience and marketing officer. “What excites us most about McLaren Racing is the culture of teamwork, resilience and continuous improvement behind every performance. Those are many of the same principles that help our clients navigate complexity and achieve what's important to them."

The 2027 NTT INDYCAR SERIES season starts Sunday, March 7 on the streets of St. Petersburg, Florida.

title: 1 day ago •Driver News INDYCAR Statement on Passing of Gordon Johncock
excerpt:
A statement from Indianapolis Motor Speedway and INDYCAR President J. Douglas Boles about two-time Indianapolis 500 winner and 1976 INDYCAR SERIES champion Gordon Johncock, who died Monday, Sept. 28 in South Branch, Michigan, at age 90:

“Gordon Johncock was known for his hard-charging, no-nonsense style of racing, and he left a lasting legacy on both Indianapolis Motor Speedway and INDYCAR. While his 1973 Indianapolis 500 victory was overshadowed by tragedy, that race was an inflection point for safety, leading to a vital shift in track engineering and regulations. Gordon was unable to truly celebrate his first win, so that made his second win in 1982, following a thrilling duel with Rick Mears, all the more memorable. His victory is one of the iconic moments in the history of the Speedway. Remembered as much for his quiet life away from racing, Gordon left a lasting impact on the world of motorsports. Our thoughts and prayers are with his family and friends.”

title: Alexander Rossi Confident of Progress After ‘Pretty Terrible Year’
excerpt:
Alexander Rossi can look at his 2026 season one of two ways: a year of enduring pain or a season of what might have been.

Rossi (photo, top), who turned 34 on Sept. 25, finished 15th in the NTT INDYCAR SERIES standings with one top-five finish and five top-10 results this season. It was a step back from 2025, his first season driving the No. 20 ECR Chevrolet, when he also finished 15th in the standings but recorded two top-five finishes and seven top-10 results.

“It's no secret that this has been a pretty terrible year for myself and the whole ECR team with the litany of issues, some out of our control, some in our control,” Rossi said. “Anything that could go wrong really did go wrong from crashes to failures of gearboxes, hybrids, engines. Some struggles being on fire in pit lane. Some lack of performance at some events. Anything that you can think of has happened to us across both cars. Just a really trying year.

“Really proud of the whole organization and everyone involved for kind of staying true to the course and fighting through a lot of adversity.”

And yet, there were glimpses of what Rossi and ECR could accomplish when everything came together. Rossi's season highlight came at Indianapolis Motor Speedway, where he qualified second for the 110th Running of the Indianapolis 500 presented by Gainbridge. A crash in practice the following day, however, left him with an injury to a finger on his left hand and a leg injury that required an outpatient procedure. He spent more than a month in a walking boot and detailed the injury and his fight to continue racing on his “Off Track with Hinch and Rossi” podcast last week.

Rossi also earned his 100th career top-10 finish this season, ending the season with 102 to his tally. One of those came in the season finale at WeatherTech Raceway Laguna Seca, where he started fourth and finished third.

“That was a great result to kind of reward that effort, just rebuild the confidence in everyone that we're capable of doing this,” Rossi said. “It's a good boost going into what's going to be a long offseason, but an important one, to make sure we execute a lot better and clean up a lot of our issues that we can control in 2027.”

That Laguna Seca result was evidence of a shift that began around midseason. Rossi credited a June test at Mid-Ohio Sports Car Course with helping ECR turn its performance in the right direction. The team still encountered plenty of issues on track afterward, but Rossi said the underlying speed was beginning to emerge.

The five races immediately before the Mid-Ohio test produced finishes of 25th, 30th, 17th, 18th and sixth. In the first five races of the season, Rossi had recorded four top-11 finishes.

“We started to uncover some shortcomings,” Rossi said. “There's two issues, two challenges: You have to identify the problem, then you have to figure out how to fix it. We were able to do that to a certain extent. There's still more to come from what we know.

“It's a huge step in the right direction. Now we have a lot of time to really understand. To really analyze and understand how it can be better will be useful coming into March.”

Rossi and his team returned to Indianapolis after the Laguna Seca race (photo, above) and initially analyzed the final six weeks of the season. They will expand that review to the entire year as the offseason progresses. The goal, Rossi said, is not a wholesale overhaul.

“I've said it often this year, that the team has done a lot of things better year over year from '25 to '26,” Rossi said. “Just unfortunately nothing really to show for it.

“I think drastic changes aren't necessary. It's a continual evolution. Just like in a car setup, there's no magic bullet. It's the same thing in putting together a season: There's not one thing you have to do; you have to do everything a little better. It's just focusing on understanding our strengths and weaknesses and executing when we can.”

ECR also has additional resources at its disposal through Ted Gelov, who joined the organization as an investment partner and co-owner before the 2025 season. Gelov, the owner of Heartland Food Products Group, brought Heartland brands Splenda and Java House to the team.

Those resources give ECR the ability to address its needs. But they also come with the understanding that closing the gap to the series' established front-running organizations takes time.

“I think the team knows now that it has the ability,” Rossi said. “If we feel we need something, we can go get it, right? But the teams that we're trying to close the gap to have had that advantage on this organization at ECR for a decade.

“Just because someone comes in and gives you the resources and tools to close that gap, the teams you're competing against don't stop developing either. You have to take bigger steps than they do. It's not a simple proposition.

“This championship has so many great drivers and teams and personnel, you don't just do that overnight. Inside the organization, everyone knows if we need something, we can go get it. It's a matter of continuing to develop and get better.

“It will come. It's a process.”

title: 2 DAYS AGO •Driver News Two-Time Indianapolis 500 Winner Gordon Johncock Dies at 90
excerpt:
Gordon Johncock, whose stirring drive late in the 1982 Indianapolis 500 earned him a second victory in “The Greatest Spectacle in Racing,” died of natural causes Sept. 28 at home in South Branch, Michigan. He was 90.

Born Aug. 5, 1936, in Hastings, Michigan, the longtime resident of the state (photo, top) was the INDYCAR SERIES national champion in 1976 and won 25 races in the series. Yet, Johncock was known for winning both memorable and forgettable “500s,” each time driving for Patrick Racing.

Johncock’s duel with Rick Mears in the closing laps of the 1982 race (photo, above) was the most thrilling to that point, prompting renowned television broadcaster Jim McKay to claim he’d “never seen anything like it.” Johncock masterfully covered Mears’ last-lap passing attempt in Turn 1, then outran the 1979 race winner to the finish line. Their margin at the checkered flag was a then-record .16 of a second, still the seventh closest ever.

Johncock later said he was fortunate to win as he hit an unfamiliar bump low in Turn 3 on the last lap that pushed his car up the track and gave Mears an opportunity to gain ground.

“I pretty near lost it,” he told The Indianapolis Star in 2016. “Ask Rick; he saw it (because) he was right there.

“I had never run that low before in Turn 3, but I knew I had to if I was going to be able to stay in the throttle. It was just a little rougher down there than I expected.”

The 1973 “500” was one of tragedy and poor weather, with rain postponing the race two days. Johncock started 11th and grabbed his first lead on Lap 40, but soon after teammate Swede Savage and crew member Armando Teran were involved in separate horrifying accidents.

Johncock, who led 64 laps, was in front of Bill Vukovich II when rain ended the race on Lap 133. With the annual Victory Banquet canceled, Johncock and his Patrick crew “celebrated” with hamburgers at a local Burger Chef restaurant after visiting Savage in the hospital.

Johncock was able to properly celebrate following his 1982 victory (photo, above), and Mears said he never felt so good finishing second.

“I remember thinking during the race that if we can’t win it would be great to see him win,” Mears said.

Said Johncock of watching replays of the duel with Mears, “It gives you goosebumps … (that) well, I did it again!”

After a successful stint as a sprint car racer, Johncock’s INDYCAR SERIES career began in 1964 with a dirt race in Springfield, Illinois, and it didn’t take him long to show his talent. Johncock finished fifth as a rookie in the 1965 “500” in a roadster (photo, above), in a race that saw five rookies finish in the top nine. He won for the first time nine races later at the Milwaukee Mile. Johncock also scored the first of his 20 career poles that year.

Johncock started his own team in 1967, joining A.J. Foyt as the sport’s only owner/driver. Johncock won six races during that three-year span.

Johncock nearly won a few more Indianapolis 500s. He finished third in 1976 and 1978, and he was fourth on two other occasions (1966 and 1974). In 1977, Johncock was leading Foyt, the eventual winner, with 16 laps remaining when his car’s crankshaft broke. He had led 129 laps.

Johncock’s career in the INDYCAR SERIES spanned 262 starts over 25 seasons. He actually retired twice, the first during the first week of “500” practice in 1985. He served on the IMS Radio Network for that race. Two years later, he replaced the injured Jim Crawford and finished 22nd.

Johncock’s last “500” was in 1992 after he retired on Lap 60 with engine failure. He finished 29th. His 24 starts in the race ranks fifth among all drivers, tied with Johnny Rutherford and Scott Dixon. Johncock led 339 laps in the Indianapolis 500, which stands 15th all time.

Johncock was one of the last living drivers to have competed in front- and rear-engine Indy cars.

He was successful in stock car racing, too, competing in 21 of NASCAR’s top-division races. He made three starts in the Daytona 500, qualifying fifth in 1973. He had three top-five finishes in NASCAR, highlighted by a fourth in the 1973 Firecracker 400 at Daytona International Speedway. He also won a pole at Atlanta Motor Speedway that season.

After Johncock’s second retirement, he turned his focus to his timber business in South Branch, Michigan, located 200 miles north of Detroit. Johncock enjoyed such a quiet life away from racing that some employees were surprised to learn he had been a race car driver, much less a two-time Indy 500 winner.

Johncock kept most of his racing memorabilia in his basement, although his two winner’s plaques have shared a wall with artwork of the 1982 win, the race’s checkered flag and a stuffed deer head in his living room. He seldom attended the “500” after retiring.

“It was a job I used to have,” Johncock said of racing. “Now I have a different job.”

Johncock was inducted into the Indianapolis Motor Speedway Hall of Fame in 1997 and the International Motorsports Hall of Fame in 1999.

Johncock is survived by his wife, Sue; three daughters (Patsy, Pamilee, Peggy), two sons (Gordon Jr., Wally); two stepdaughters (Traci, Valerie); and 12 grandchildren, 17 great-grandchildren and one great-great grandchild.

title: Five Drivers Who Were Better Than 2026 Standings Indicated
excerpt:
Legendary NFL head coach Bill Parcells was fond of saying “you are what your record says you are.” Generally, that’s true, but there can be exceptions.

In this year’s NTT INDYCAR SERIES, several drivers ended the season lower in the standings than their competitiveness throughout the year would suggest.

Some good runs are spoiled by unfortunate luck, and the average becomes the average. The finish of the five drivers below would seem to be better than they became.

David Malukas

It speaks to the competitiveness at the top of the series that the driver of Team Penske’s No. 12 Chevrolet finished fifth in the standings. He consistently performed better than that and was second in points heading into August.

Malukas registered four runner-up finishes, highlighted by his position in the thrilling Indianapolis 500 presented by Gainbridge. He lost that race by .0233 of a second – the closest margin in “500” history. He also finished second in the Sonsio Grand Prix on the Indianapolis Motor Speedway road course, the XPEL Grand Prix at Road America and the back end of the doubleheader at the Milwaukee Mile, the Snap-on Makers and Fixers 250.

The Chicago-area native posted six top-three finishes, a total which ranked only behind the seven of series champion Alex Palou of Chip Ganassi Racing and third-place finisher Christian Lundgaard of Arrow McLaren.

Malukas had a run of 10 top-eight finishes in 11 races from his third-place finish in the Good Ranchers 250 at Phoenix Raceway to the Borchetta Bourbon Music City Grand Prix at Nashville Superspeedway, and he excelled on the ovals, posting a qualifying average of 3.2 and a finishing average of 3.5 while leading nearly 18 percent of the laps (255 of 1,435).

Why did Malukas not finish higher? He had five results of 12th or worse, including a stretch of August road and street races where he finished 12th, 17th and 24th as he dealt with the past wrist injury that he aggravated.

Felix Rosenqvist

The Swede’s results were so good at times that it’s perplexing that he finished ninth in the standings.

From winning the seventh and eighth poles of his career to that spectacular last lap to win the Indianapolis 500 to finishing second in the Acura Grand Prix of Long Beach and the OnlyBulls Grand Prix of Portland, Rosenqvist’s good days were great.

The driver of Meyer Shank Racing w/ Curb Agajanian’s No. 60 Honda also led nine of the 18 races during the season.

What evened things out were 11 double-digit finishes, including the first four races of the season and five of the first six races.

Will Power

The transition to Andretti Global’s No. 26 Honda was marred by an unfortunate start to the season, with an average finish of 17.0 through the first eight races. However, Power led five of those races, including a front-row start for the Chevrolet Detroit Grand Prix, so it often was a case of suffering bad luck in one form or another.

Power settled in well in the second half of the season, posting three consecutive third-place finishes in August to finish 11th in the standings.

Power led 12 of the 18 races, finishing third on five occasions. Five podium finishes were bettered only by Palou and Lundgaard (seven each) and the six of Malukas and Andretti Global teammate Kyle Kirkwood. That would seem to set the two-time series champion up well for 2027.

Marcus Armstrong

A driver who led the Indianapolis 500 coming to the white flag had a stronger season than a 14th-place finish would suggest.

Armstrong (photo, top) had several strong runs, highlighted by fifth-place finishes on the ovals at Phoenix and Indianapolis. The driver of Meyer Shank Racing w/ Curb Agajanian’s No. 66 Honda also finished sixth in the Children’s of Alabama Indy Grand Prix at Barber Motorsports Park and ended the season with a pair of top-10 finishes (ninth in the second Milwaukee race, seventh in the Mission Foods Grand Prix of Monterey at WeatherTech Raceway Laguna Seca).

The Kiwi’s position in the standings was the result of a run of seven midseason races where he had an average finish of 19.7, and at least three of those were due to mechanical failures.

Armstrong is moving to the lead role at MSR for next season, and it’s not a stretch to expect him to finish much higher in the standings.

Graham Rahal

Rahal was so strong on road courses this season that it’s easy to forget his struggles on short ovals.

The veteran of Rahal Letterman Lanigan Racing’s No. 15 Honda posted third-place finishes at Barber Motorsports Park and the Sonsio Grand Prix while running third two corners from the finish in the XPEL Grand Prix at Road America (Power knocked him off the track, resulting in a 23rd-place finish). Rahal also finished third in the street race in Detroit.

But after showing well at Phoenix early in the year – he qualified third and finished ninth – Rahal had an average finish of 21.8 on the four ensuing short ovals, and his 20th-place finish in the “500” wasn’t up to his usually competitive standards.

The result was a 16th-place standings finish.

title: Final Statistics Betray Graham Rahal’s Progress This Season
excerpt:
Driver News

6 DAYS AGO

Graham Rahal’s rocky NTT INDYCAR SERIES season was capsulized by the last-lap happenings in the XPEL Grand Prix at Road America on June 21.

Rahal had passed Will Power for third place in Turn 6 only to have Power’s trailing car make contact with his approaching Turn 12. The impact sent Rahal sliding to the outside barrier, where it ricocheted into the gravel barrier.

Rahal (photo, top) had been on pace to be the highest-finishing Honda driver. Instead, it was a crushing 23rd-place finish.

“Two corners away from (a podium finish),” Rahal said with a sigh at the season-ending event at WeatherTech Raceway Laguna Seca.

Rahal’s results in the 18-race campaign included a healthy amount of feast and more than his share of famine. The driver of Rahal Letterman Lanigan Racing’s No. 15 Honda had three top-three finishes, but they were offset by six finishes in the 20s, including the one at Road America that could have been in the former category.

Only six drivers had more podium finishes, and had Power not knocked him sideways at Road America, he would have matched Team Penske’s Scott McLaughlin in that category. Series champion Alex Palou of Chip Ganassi Racing and Arrow McLaren’s Christian Lundgaard led the series with seven podiums each, while Andretti Global’s Kyle Kirkwood and Team Penske’s David Malukas had six apiece. Andretti Global’s Power had five.

Rahal’s podium finishes came in the Children’s of Alabama Indy Grand Prix at Barber Motorsports Park (photo, above), the Sonsio Grand Prix on the Indianapolis Motor Speedway road course and the Chevrolet Detroit Grand Prix. He qualified third and finished ninth in the Good Ranchers 250 at Phoenix Raceway in the season’s second race. In street racing, he qualified and finished ninth in the Ontario Honda Dealers Indy at Markham, Ontario, and led a season-high 12 laps in the Freedom 250 Grand Prix of Washington, D.C.

Yet, despite how well Rahal and his RLL crew performed in some events, their struggles at others left them 16th in the standings.

“So, while people want to discount us, I don't think that that's necessarily fair on a year like this year,” Rahal said. “We had a lot of good opportunities, but what our weakness was on one weekend we'd be on the podium, the next weekend we'd finish 23rd.

“Our highs were high, our lows were very, very low, and that's the frustration for me.”

Another example of that was in the August weekend in the OnlyBulls Grand Prix at Portland. Rahal qualified eighth – “(That position was) way better than I thought I was going to qualify,” he said – but he finished a lap off the pace in 23rd place.

“So, things like that (were) quite frustrating,” he said.

The six-time race winner in this series had already turned his focus to next season by the time the series arrived at WeatherTech Raceway Laguna Seca for the Mission Foods Grand Prix of Monterey, the last race of the year. There, Rahal said he and the team will have their short oval package high on the list of areas to improve given their struggles at Nashville Superspeedway and the Milwaukee Mile in the second half of the season.

“I’m very decided to (2027) already to try to make sure we’re making the right moves, doing the right things,” Rahal said, adding that RLL will reset with two full-season entries (for Rahal and Louis Foster). “We’ve tried to keep up this three-car thing for many years, often at the great expense of our team owners. Just need to reset and rethink.

“It’s a very important time of the year to make sure that we're doing the right things.”

title: Indianapolis 500 Folk Hero ‘Jigger’ Sirois Dies at 91
excerpt:
Leon Duray “Jigger” Sirois, who became part of Indianapolis 500 folklore by nearly earning an improbable pole for the 1969 race, died Sept. 23. He was 91.

Sirois, a native of Shelby, Indiana, made no starts in “The Greatest Spectacle in Racing” despite attempting to qualify every year from 1969-75. But his close call at earning the top starting spot in unique circumstances in May 1969 became a legendary story in the history of the world’s greatest race.

Midget car standout Sirois drew first in line to attempt to qualify on Pole Day, May 17, 1969, in the No. 14 Gerhardt-Offenhauser owned by California car dealer Myron Caves. After a long rain delay, Sirois entered the 2.5-mile oval late in the afternoon to make the first four-lap qualification attempt of the day.

His first three laps ranged between 160 and 162 mph, but Caves waved off the final lap of the run due to a perceived lack of speed, negating the run. Moments later, Arnie Knepper began his qualifying attempt, but rain began to fall during his warmup laps and continued, washing out all track activity for the rest of the weekend.

If Sirois’ final lap had not been waved off, he would have been the lone qualifier of the weekend and have sat on the coveted provisional pole for that week, perhaps even holding it through Bump Day the next weekend and starting the race from the top spot. Sirois’ second and third attempts the next weekend also were waved off due to lack of speed or mechanical problems, and he didn’t qualify for the race.

Qualification rules were changed in 1971 to guarantee all cars in line on the first day of qualifying at least one chance to make the field during the first round, ending any chance of another “Jigger” story.

Sirois continued to attempt to qualify for the “500” every year through 1975, including the sluggish Jack Adams Turbine in 1970. It was the last qualifying attempt ever for the Indianapolis 500 by a turbine-engine car. He was the second alternate for the 1974 race, falling just short of making the field.

The failure to qualify at Indianapolis belied Sirois’ skill at many levels of open-wheel racing.

Sirois failed to qualify for the five USAC Champ Car races he entered in 1967 driving for team owner Bob Cavanaugh. But he attracted strong attention from Indianapolis 500 car owners in 1968 after he was forced to withdraw from the inaugural USAC Champ Car race at Michigan International Speedway due to clutch failure while running as high as second in low-budget equipment.

He made 10 USAC Champ Car starts, with a best finish of fifth in 1969 at Phoenix. He also finished third – in a turbine-engine car – behind winner A.J. Foyt and Knepper in the rain-shortened Ted Horn Memorial USAC National Dirt Car Championship race in September 1972 at DuQuoin, Illinois.

Sirois enjoyed the most success in midgets, primarily racing around the Chicago area. He won four championships in 1961, including the UARA midget title. He was inducted into the National Midget Racing Hall of Fame in 2013.

One of the most popular veteran drivers, Sirois returned to IMS in May frequently to meet fans and media members, always well-liked for his geniality and courtesy. His sportsmanship surrounding the fateful decision to wave off his 1969 qualifying attempt – he never once blamed Caves or his crew – led the American Auto Racing Writers & Broadcasters Association (AARWBA) to create the annual “Jigger Award” to honor the year’s “hard luck” driver during qualifying. Sirois was the first recipient in 1969.

Sirois was born into the sport. His father, Earl “Frenchy” Sirois, was a longtime Indianapolis 500 mechanic who worked on the winning cars of Lee Wallard, Sam Hanks and Jimmy Bryan during his 40-year career. Sirois was named after two-time “500” pole winner Leon Duray.

The legendary nickname “Jigger” referred to two-time Indy 500-winning riding mechanic Jigger Johnson, a family friend. Sirois’ older sister also called him by that name.

Sirois suffered from a stutter that began during a tornado scare near his hometown of Shelby when he was 3 years old. He began to manage his stutter in his mid-60s after receiving speech therapy and worked tirelessly to promote awareness and treatment of stuttering disorders in youth.

title: Inside Line: 2026 Moment That Will Matter Most in 2027?
excerpt:
Featured

7 DAYS AGO

Today’s question: What moment from the 2026 NTT INDYCAR SERIES season will matter the most in the 2027 season?

Curt Cavin: I’d like to highlight a stretch of late-season races where Will Power earned three consecutive podium finishes (third each at Portland, Markham and Washington). That was part of seven races in a row in which Power (photo, above) led laps, and he ended the year with five top-three finishes, the fifth-highest individual total and only two off that of series champion Alex Palou. Why is it important to single out three races of a driver who finished 11th in the point standings? Because Power is a two-time series champion who figures to be massively confident heading into his second season with Andretti Global. Even if Power doesn’t win a third title, he can be the help teammate Kyle Kirkwood needs to overthrow Palou. It’s worth noting that Andretti Global’s combination of Kirkwood, Power and Marcus Ericsson combined for 13 podium finishes, tied with Team Penske for the most among teams in 2026. Don’t be surprised if they gang up on Palou next season.

Eric Smith: I think the way David Malukas lost the Indy 500 in May could help him win the “500” next year. That’s my moment because the final lap of this past year’s Indy 500 is arguably the moment of the entire 2026 season. Alex Palou admitted that his 2021 Indy 500 defeat to Helio Castroneves taught him what he needed to know to win the 2025 race. Malukas (photo, above) came close -- finishing as the closest second-place finisher in Indy 500 history. It was also his second consecutive runner-up finish in the race. Thirty-six drivers have finished second in the Indy 500 and gone on to win it, with nine of those drivers earning their runner-up finish the year before their first “500” victory. Now, with Malukas driving a Team Penske car, he should be in contention. More importantly, he has the experience and knowledge from his recent defeats to close the deal and capture the 2027 Indy 500 victory.

Arni Sribhen: For me, it’s the driver movement at Arrow McLaren and Chip Ganassi Racing — a sequence of moves that could turn three separate moments into one massive storyline, with the biggest piece still waiting to fall into place. At the center of it: Scott Dixon and Christian Lundgaard. Call it a “trade” if you want, because that’s exactly how this is going to be viewed. Sure, both teams still have nine other organizations to race next season. But make no mistake, every Lundgaard result at his new home will be measured against what Dixon (photo, above) does at his. And if Lundgaard follows up with another title-contending season? The comparisons will get loud. Then there’s the history. These two organizations aren’t exactly exchanging Christmas cards. The Alex Palou saga made that clear, and there’s been no shortage of bad blood – particularly between the people running the show. So, keep an eye on this one. Because by the end of 2027, when we look back at the Dixon-Lundgaard “trade,” one of these organizations could be doing a whole lot more laughing than the other.

Paul Kelly: The success of the new street races in Arlington and Washington rank very high for me, both short term and long term. In the short view, the Java House Grand Prix of Arlington (photo, top) will continue to prosper and grow into one of the NTT INDYCAR SERIES’ tentpole events next season. Don’t be surprised if it ranks with the Acura Grand Prix of Long Beach as one of the series’ unofficial “majors” besides the Indianapolis 500 presented by Gainbridge. While it’s unlikely the series returns to Washington next year, the overwhelming success of that race provides a template for excellence for promoters of every street race in the series, and you can be sure those lessons will be applied elsewhere. Plus, INDYCAR stages street races arguably better than any series in North America, and that successful model can be borrowed from Arlington and Washington and taken to another city. The series badly needs a race in the Northeast, so the streets of Philadelphia (sorry, Bruce Springsteen!), anyone? How about a Mile High fight on the streets of Denver?

title: ‘500’ Reality Sinks In for Felix Rosenqvist After Seeing Borg Likeness
excerpt:
Felix Rosenqvist traveled to Tryon, North Carolina, this week to see his face that will be added to one of the most exclusive pieces of hardware in motorsports.

On Sept. 22, artist William Behrends unveiled Rosenqvist’s sculpted clay likeness that will serve as the bas-relief portrait on the Borg-Warner Trophy. The iconic hardware carries the likeness of every Indianapolis 500 winner, creating a visual history of the race dating to its inaugural running in 1911.

“It’s been quite the experience,” Rosenqvist said. “Such a cool, unique little trip here, getting to meet Will (Behrends) and his family. It’s kind of a rare thing to experience. I never thought I would be sculpted. I think it’s not a thing people really expect to do in their lifetime.

“He did a hell of a job with it. To do all the details right was very impressive to see. Even my little imperfections we all have, they’re all there.”

Rosenqvist earned his place on the Borg-Warner Trophy by winning the 110th Running of the Indianapolis 500 presented by Gainbridge on May 24. Driving the No. 60 SiriusXM Honda for Meyer Shank Racing w/Curb Agajanian, he made a daring move on the final lap, riding the high line against the wall exiting Turn 4 on Lap 200 and powering past David Malukas in the No. 12 Verizon Team Penske Chevrolet just yards before the Yard of Bricks start-finish line.

Rosenqvist won by .0233 of a second, the closest finish in Indianapolis 500 history. The race also featured a record-setting 70 lead changes. The victory came in Rosenqvist’s eighth Indianapolis 500 start, made him the 77th different winner of the race and earned him a record $4.34 million in prize money.

His victory initially took him on a media tour before the NTT INDYCAR SERIES returned to competition the following weekend on the streets of Detroit. With the season over, Rosenqvist said the trip to Tryon felt like “celebration 2.0.”

“It becomes more real now,” Rosenqvist said. “It’s one of those kind of victories that just always stays. No one’s ever going to be able to take it away from you, which I think is also why it’s such a relief to win this race, because we all dream about it, we all think about it, but we all know also how hard to win it.

“So, when you finally get it, it’s just like such a relief, and the fact that you also get imprinted on a trophy doesn’t hurt. Like, no one can undo what you did.”

Now, Rosenqvist is part of that history. He also brings a distinction no previous winner has brought to the trophy: He is the first Indianapolis 500 winner depicted with a full beard.

“That’s almost unbelievable,” Behrends said. “I mean, how can that happen? It’s just astounding.”

Behrends, who began sculpting drivers for the Borg-Warner Trophy in 1990, wanted the beard represented without making it the first feature people noticed.

“I had to kind of play around with the clay and figure out how I was going to do that, but I think we got it,” he said.

Rosenqvist found the distinction of being the first bearded driver on the Borg as crazy but believes he became a trendsetter.

“I think it’s the most mind-blowing fact because I feel like everyone has a beard,” Rosenqvist said. “Like, out of my friends, probably at least half of them have a beard.”

Six previous winners have been depicted with mustaches: Jules Goux (1913), René Thomas (1914), Gaston Chevrolet (1920), Wilbur Shaw (1937, 1939, 1940), Mauri Rose (1941, 1947, 1948) and Bobby Rahal (1986). None had a beard.

Behrends has sculpted two other Swedish Indianapolis 500 winners, 1999 winner Kenny Brack and 2022 winner Marcus Ericsson. American Josef Newgarden won back-to-back years in 2023 and 2024 while Spaniard Alex Palou won in 2025. Rosenqvist’s likeness gave him another opportunity to capture details that make each driver unique.

“One thing I like about his face, Felix has got a very strong jaw,” Behrends said. “He has a very Swedish jaw, so I like that. It’s a very strong, kind of angular face, a different-shaped face, by far, than Alex (Palou) or Josef’s (Newgarden), but very strong.

“Then he says: ‘I got his nose right. That’s a family nose.’ Apparently, his grandfather, father and now his daughter have that nose.”

Rosenqvist also noticed another detail Behrends captured: His right ear sits slightly higher than his left. He also was blown away seeing his likeness in three dimensions. That made the experience more personal than simply seeing his name on a trophy.

“I think the details are what make it come alive,” Rosenqvist said. “Because that’s literally what makes you, you. I think the cool thing was because we’ve all seen pictures of ourselves, but to see like a 3D version of yourself and to be able to look around and walk behind him, look out behind the ears and all the kind of things you never could do, it’s a little bit of an eerie experience.

“He’s definitely a pro, and he made it definitely worthy to be on the trophy.”

The significance extends beyond Rosenqvist himself. He and his wife, Emille, welcomed their first child, Stella, in May. Rosenqvist showed his likeness to his wife on a live phone video during the studio visit (photo, above).

Rosenqvist hopes his place on the Borg-Warner Trophy, which is housed daily at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway Hall of Fame Museum, will eventually become part of his family’s connection to the race.

“Maybe our grandkids will go check it out every now and then, or maybe it’ll be a tradition where we go to Indy if we don’t live there,” Rosenqvist said. “It’ll be a cool little family thing for us.

“Whatever happens, if my daughter or if I have a son in the future, or whatever happens, they decide to do something completely different, we always have that piece of history in our family to go back and say, ‘Hey, your grandpa did that,’ which is very rare to have that possibility. It’s very unique to have that opportunity.”

Photo credits: Scott R. LePage

title: Scott Dixon To Drive No. 6, Felix Rosenqvist No. 7 for Arrow McLaren
excerpt:
Pato O’Ward Staying in No. 5, Ryan Hunter-Reay Back in No. 31 at Indy

The Arrow McLaren IndyCar Team announced Sept. 23 its driver numbers for its new lineup entering the 2027 NTT INDYCAR SERIES season.

Pato O'Ward will continue in the No. 5, while Scott Dixon will take over the No. 6 entry, and Felix Rosenqvist will drive the No. 7. In the team's additional Indy 500 entry, Ryan Hunter-Reay will continue with the No. 31 next May.

Additionally, Arrow McLaren unveiled a new font style for car numbers in line with the rebrand McLaren Racing rolled out Sept. 22 that will go into effect in January 2027.

"We're excited to begin our next chapter in 2027," Team Principal Tony Kanaan said. "This team has continued to raise the bar year after year, and with Pato, Scott, Felix and Ryan in the cockpit, we believe we have the tools to achieve our goals. While fans will have to wait a little longer to see the 2027 liveries, today's announcement offers a fun glimpse of what lies ahead."

Dixon is set to sport a new car number in INDYCAR SERIES competition for the first time in more than two decades after competing in his familiar No. 9 for all but one of the past 24 seasons (No. 1 in 2004). Fresh off his Indianapolis 500 presented by Gainbridge victory in 2026, Rosenqvist returns to the No. 7 entry, the same number he drove during his first two seasons with Arrow McLaren from 2021-22.

The 2027 NTT INDYCAR SERIES season starts Sunday, March 7 in St. Petersburg, Florida.

title: Historic Season Unleashes New Era of Growth for NTT INDYCAR SERIES
excerpt:
The 2026 NTT INDYCAR SERIES season was historic, record-breaking and game-changing for North America’s premier open-wheel racing series. From massive audience gains to soaring attendance, booming digital engagement and world-class competition, the series leaped forward into a new position of prominence and impact across the sporting landscape.

“This is an incredible new era for the NTT INDYCAR SERIES, defined by growth, energy and momentum,” Penske Entertainment President & CEO Mark Miles said. “Our partnership with FOX Sports has raised the bar for our sport, and in turn we’ve invested in new events and opportunities to accelerate our already immense progress. Alongside our teams and partners, our commitment to maintain and expand one of the fastest growth curves in all of sports is unmatched.”

A look at the season, by the facts and numbers:

Surging Viewership

The NTT INDYCAR SERIES reached an average audience of 1.68 million viewers on FOX across an 18-race schedule. This represents the largest average viewership in almost two decades, dating back to the 2008 season. In total, nine races saw an average audience of more than 1 million viewers, also the most since the 2008 season.

The historic Freedom 250 Grand Prix of Washington, D.C. provided particularly stellar viewership, reaching a peak audience of 3.5 million people. This was the highest tune-in for a non-Indy 500 race since 1995. With all coverage on FOX combined, the NTT INDYCAR SERIES made a record 23 appearances on broadcast television in 2026.

Rising Attendance

Race weekend attendance increased by approximately 20 percent, benchmarked by another grandstand sellout at the Indianapolis 500 presented by Gainbridge and a massive crowd of 215,000 people across the Freedom 250 Grand Prix race weekend.

Additional highlights included a record-breaking weekend at the Firestone Grand Prix of St. Petersburg and a record-tying weekend at the Acura Grand Prix of Long Beach. INDYCAR’s return to Phoenix Raceway resulted in doubled Saturday attendance for the promoter and additional buzz surrounding an action-packed motorsport weekend. The inaugural Java House Grand Prix of Arlington also declared a grandstand sellout on race morning, highlighting incredible interest in the new event powered by a joint venture between INDYCAR, the Dallas Cowboys and REV Entertainment.

Impressive Digital Gains

INDYCAR’s social channels reached new heights in 2026, led by notable milestones in engagement and video consumption. The 2026 Indianapolis 500 presented by Gainbridge delivered the most popular digital day in NTT INDYCAR SERIES history, with more than 1.5 million engagements. In addition, there were more than 250 million video views across social and digital channels, also a new record.

The INDYCAR App powered by NTT DATA delivered a record-breaking performance in 2026 with the highest-ever average race day users across the season and a nearly 20 percent increase in screen views compared to 2025. The immersive relationship with NTT also celebrated a monumental moment in May, as NTT, Inc., together with NTT DATA Group Corporation, announced continued sponsorship of the NTT INDYCAR SERIES.

INDYCAR’s YouTube channel saw significant growth for the 2026 season with a 58 percent increase in watch time, a 41 percent increase in view duration and a nearly 70 percent growth in livestream views.

The new, digital-first docuseries “ALL IN: INDYCAR” also expanded the sport’s dedicated shoulder programming and reached a new and younger audience. Produced by INDYCAR in tandem with FOX Sports and Tom Brady’s Shadow Lion, “ALL IN: INDYCAR” racked up more than 6 million views on YouTube, averaging almost 500,000 views an episode.

Merchandise Sales Soar

NTT INDYCAR SERIES merchandise flew off the shelves across the season, with a nearly 40 percent increase in race weekend sales. The series set a new non-Indy 500 sales record in Arlington, only to break it months later on the streets of Washington. New and expanded lines were unveiled with brands such as Homefield, True Brand, Flag & Anthem, Under Armour, Travis Matthew, Lululemon and more.

World-Class Competition

The NTT INDYCAR SERIES once again featured intense, high-speed drama and competition, powered by a global field of elite drivers. Chip Ganassi Racing’s Alex Palou, at just 29 years old, became the youngest five-time champion in INDYCAR SERIES history. Meyer Shank Racing w/Curb Agajanian’s Felix Rosenqvist earned his first Indy 500 victory in the closest finish in the race’s storied century-plus history.

Competition remained fierce throughout the 18-race schedule, with eight different drivers winning races and a record 20 drivers making at least one Firestone Fast Six qualifying appearance. In total, nine different race teams were represented on the podium in 2026.

IR-28 Unveiled

With momentum on its side, the NTT INDYCAR SERIES also showcased its commitment to the future with the unveiling of the IR-28 car that will be introduced for the start of the 2028 season. Lighter, faster and built to break track records, the IR-28 will encourage more wheel-to-wheel action through improved raceability, while its innovative and modern design will also engage a new generation of fans.

“The IR-28 unveil was a massive milestone for the sport, and it has been incredible to get so much positive feedback from both our drivers and our fans,” INDYCAR President J. Douglas Boles said. “To capitalize on our momentum, we need to be constantly innovating and look toward the future, and the IR-28 reflects our commitment to this mindset.”

The IR-28 also showcases the continued commitment of Chevy and Honda as INDYCAR’s Official Engine Manufacturers (OEM). The 2026 calendar year started with news that both partners had committed to new OEM agreements running multiple years, reflecting the upward trajectory of the sport and continued investments in its growth.

Stay tuned for more NTT INDYCAR SERIES updates as the sport turns the page on the 2026 season and prepares for an action-packed and highly anticipated 2027.

title: Scott McLaughlin Pleased To Complete Road Back to Victory Lane
excerpt:
Scott McLaughlin never doubted he would return to victory lane. The question was, how long it would take?

McLaughlin ended the longest winless streak of his professional racing career earlier this month in the NTT INDYCAR SERIES’ season finale at WeatherTech Raceway Laguna Seca. The victory snapped a 36-race drought that capped a season of rebuilding for the New Zealander and Team Penske.

The road back began long before the checkered flag fell at Laguna Seca. McLaughlin entered the 2025 Indianapolis 500 presented by Gainbridge fifth in the championship standings, only 14 points behind Kyle Kirkwood for second place. McLaughlin had four top-six finishes in the opening five races and appeared to be a legitimate championship contender.

Then everything changed. Series officials discovered illegal attenuators on the cars of teammates Will Power and Josef Newgarden before Indianapolis 500 qualifying. The fallout led to the departures of team president Tim Cindric, managing director Ron Ruzewski and general manager Kyle Moyer.

Moyer was McLaughlin’s strategist. Cindric and Ruzewski had been calling strategy for Newgarden and Power, respectively. The changes impacted all three cars as the organization worked to rebuild its competition structure. Team Penske eventually found its footing, winning two of the final three races of the 2025 season, one by Power the other by Newgarden, but the transition carried into the offseason.

More changes followed before the start of 2026. Jonathan Diuguid shed the interim label and became Team Penske president. He also moved into the strategist role for Newgarden, with Luke Mason transitioning to engineer. Ben Bretzman, McLaughlin’s longtime engineer since he came to the series for the 2020 season finale and full-time from 2021 onward, took on an engineering management role across all three cars.

For the first time in his NTT INDYCAR SERIES career, McLaughlin had a new race engineer in Raul Prados. He also had a new spotter in David Hunt. Cindric returned for race weekends as McLaughlin’s strategist.

Prados brought extensive sports car experience to the No. 3 Team Penske Chevrolet. He had been competing in the IMSA WeatherTech SportsCar Championship since 2017 and was part of a championship-winning program before returning to INDYCAR competition. The adjustment took time.

“This is the most competitive category I've ever been in in my life as well,” McLaughlin said. “Even more so than any of the years of Supercars and stuff. I think this category is super tough right now, super tight and you need everything to go right.”

The breakthrough came with a late-June test at Mid-Ohio Sports Car Course. With limited testing opportunities, a full day’s worth of work allowed the team to fix a communication barrier.

McLaughlin (photo, above) had six top-10 finishes through the first 10 races of the season entering that test and an average finish of 9.3. Over the final eight races, his average finish improved to eighth despite a 22nd-place result in Washington, where he crashed while battling Kirkwood for the lead with fewer than 20 laps remaining. Remove that result and the numbers tell an even better story. McLaughlin’s average finish over the final eight races would have been 5.5.

The improvement was not simply a matter of results. The No. 3 team began giving McLaughlin a car capable of competing at the front on different types of circuits.

McLaughlin finished fourth at Portland International Raceway and second and fourth in the doubleheader at the Milwaukee Mile before breaking through with season finale win. The run gave McLaughlin three consecutive top-four finishes to close the season and, perhaps more importantly, confidence that the pieces were finally coming together.

Perhaps the biggest piece was he and Prado’s communication.

McLaughlin knows he can be fiery on the radio. Prados was still learning how to translate those messages into changes on the car. Sometimes, McLaughlin’s fiery description of a problem led Prados to make a larger adjustment than necessary.

A car that was already capable of running at the front might need a small change to remain there. Instead, the team occasionally made a larger swing in search of the solution. They eventually found a better way to communicate.

“We went back to the old printed-off track maps, and I marked on each section of the track where it was really bad or a 10 out of 10 and put it in the truck good,” McLaughlin said.

It was a simple solution to a complicated problem. Instead of relying solely on radio conversations during the intensity of a race weekend, McLaughlin and Prados created a shared language for identifying where the car needed work and how much work it needed. That process helped turn a new driver-engineer pairing into one capable of fighting at the front. The result was visible at Laguna Seca.

The victory did more than close a difficult chapter. It provided evidence that the changes inside Team Penske were beginning to produce the results everyone expected from one of INDYCAR’s premier organizations.

“I think we're getting our way back to where we want to be,” McLaughlin said.
